----------------------------------------------------------------------
This is the API documentation for the fastapi_chameleon library.
----------------------------------------------------------------------


## Setup

Point the library at your Chameleon templates folder once at app startup.


global_init(template_folder: str | ForwardRef('os.PathLike[str]'), auto_reload: bool = False, cache_init: bool = True) -> None

Initialize the Chameleon template engine for your app.

Call this once at startup, pointing it at the folder that holds your ``*.pt``
templates. Template paths used elsewhere (in ``template()``, ``response()``,
``not_found()``, and ``generic_error()``) are resolved relative to this folder.
Call it before the modules that define decorated views are imported, so that
template name inference sees the right folder.

Example::

    from pathlib import Path
    import fastapi_chameleon

    templates = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / 'templates'
    fastapi_chameleon.global_init(templates, auto_reload=dev_mode)

:param template_folder: Path to the folder containing your Chameleon templates, as a
    ``str`` or any ``os.PathLike`` such as ``pathlib.Path``.
:param bool auto_reload: Reload templates from disk when they change. Handy in
    development; leave ``False`` in production. Defaults to ``False``.
:param bool cache_init: When ``True`` (the default), a second call is a no-op once
    the engine is already initialized. Pass ``False`` to force re-initialization
    (for example, to switch template folders in tests).
:raises FastAPIChameleonException: If ``template_folder`` is empty or is not a directory.


## Rendering views

Decorate FastAPI view functions to render templates, or build a response directly.


template(template_file: Callable[..., ~R] | str | None = None, mimetype: str = 'text/html')

Decorate a FastAPI view to render its return value through a Chameleon template.

Works on both sync and async view functions, and can be used three ways::

    @template('home/index.pt')   # explicit template file
    @template()                  # infer the template name
    @template                    # bare form, also infers the name

When no template file is given, the name is inferred as ``{module}/{function}``
under the template folder (the module's last dotted segment and the view's name),
preferring a ``.html`` file and falling back to ``.pt``.

The decorated view should return a ``dict`` (used as the template's variables). If
it returns a ``fastapi.Response`` instead, the template is skipped and the response
is passed through unchanged. Returning anything else raises
``FastAPIChameleonException``.

Example::

    @app.get('/')
    @fastapi_chameleon.template('home/index.pt')
    def index():
        return {'title': 'Home'}

:param template_file: The Chameleon template file (path relative to the template
    folder). Omit it (or pass ``None``) to infer the name from the view. In the bare
    ``@template`` form this argument receives the view function itself.
:param str mimetype: The response media type. Defaults to ``text/html``.
:return: The decorated view (bare form) or a decorator to apply to the view.

response(template_file: str, mimetype: str = 'text/html', status_code: int = 200, **template_data) -> starlette.responses.Response

Render a template and return it as a FastAPI response directly.

Use this when you want a rendered ``Response`` without the ``template()``
decorator, for example to return a fully-formed response from a view that does
its own branching. Requires ``global_init()`` to have been called first.

Example::

    @app.get('/sitemap.xml')
    def sitemap():
        return fastapi_chameleon.response('seo/sitemap.pt', mimetype='application/xml', urls=load_urls())

:param str template_file: The Chameleon template file to render (path relative to
    the template folder, ``*.pt``).
:param str mimetype: The response media type. Defaults to ``text/html``.
:param int status_code: The HTTP status code for the response. Defaults to ``200``.
:param template_data: Keyword arguments passed through to the template as variables.
:return: A ``fastapi.Response`` containing the rendered template, with the given
    media type and status code.
:raises FastAPIChameleonException: If ``global_init()`` has not been called.


## Error responses

Short-circuit a view to render a friendly error page with the right status code.


not_found(four04template_file: str = 'errors/404.pt') -> NoReturn

Short-circuit the current view and render a friendly 404 page.

Call this from inside a ``template()``-decorated view when a resource cannot be
found. It raises an exception that the decorator catches and turns into an HTTP
404 response rendered from ``four04template_file``. This function never returns
normally.

Example::

    @app.get('/items/{item_id}')
    @fastapi_chameleon.template('catalog/item.pt')
    def item(item_id: int):
        item = repo.get(item_id)
        if not item:
            fastapi_chameleon.not_found()
        return {'item': item}

:param str four04template_file: The template to render for the 404 response (path
    relative to the template folder). Defaults to ``errors/404.pt``.
:raises FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException: Always; this is how the 404 is signalled
    to the decorator.

generic_error(template_file: str, status_code: int, template_data: dict | None = None) -> NoReturn

Short-circuit the current view and render an error page with a custom status code.

Like ``not_found()``, but for any error: call it from inside a
``template()``-decorated view to render ``template_file`` with the HTTP
``status_code`` you choose (for example ``401`` or ``500``). The decorator catches
the raised exception and builds the response. This function never returns normally.

Example::

    if not user.is_admin:
        fastapi_chameleon.generic_error('errors/403.pt', 403, template_data={'user': user})

:param str template_file: The error template to render (path relative to the
    template folder).
:param int status_code: The HTTP status code to return (for example
    ``fastapi.status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED``).
:param dict template_data: Optional variables passed to the template. Defaults to
    ``None`` (an empty context).
:raises FastAPIChameleonGenericException: Always; this is how the error is signalled
    to the decorator.


## Exceptions

Exception types raised by the library (the error helpers raise these internally).


FastAPIChameleonException

Base class for every error raised by fastapi-chameleon.

Raised directly for configuration and rendering problems, such as calling
``global_init()`` with a missing or invalid template folder, rendering before
``global_init()`` has run, or returning an unsupported type from a decorated view.
The control-flow exceptions below subclass it, so catching this type catches them all.

Example::

    try:
        fastapi_chameleon.global_init(settings.template_folder)
    except FastAPIChameleonException as e:
        raise SystemExit(f'Template folder problem: {e}')

FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException(message: str | None = None, four04template_file: str = 'errors/404.pt')

Signals a 404 response from inside a decorated view.

Raised by ``not_found()`` and caught by the ``template()`` decorator, which renders
``template_file`` with an HTTP 404 status. You normally raise it indirectly via
``not_found()`` rather than constructing it yourself.

Example::

    try:
        fastapi_chameleon.not_found('errors/custom_404.pt')
    except FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException as e:
        assert e.template_file == 'errors/custom_404.pt'

:ivar template_file: The template to render for the 404 response (the constructor
    accepts it as ``four04template_file``).
:vartype template_file: str
:ivar message: The optional human-readable message describing the error.
:vartype message: Optional[str]

FastAPIChameleonGenericException(template_file: str, status_code: int, message: str | None = None, template_data: dict | None = None)

Signals an arbitrary error response from inside a decorated view.

Raised by ``generic_error()`` and caught by the ``template()`` decorator, which
renders ``template_file`` with the chosen ``status_code``. You normally raise it
indirectly via ``generic_error()`` rather than constructing it yourself.

Example::

    try:
        fastapi_chameleon.generic_error('errors/403.pt', 403, template_data={'user': user})
    except FastAPIChameleonGenericException as e:
        assert e.status_code == 403 and e.template_data == {'user': user}

:ivar template_file: The template to render for the error response.
:vartype template_file: str
:ivar status_code: The HTTP status code to return.
:vartype status_code: int
:ivar message: The optional human-readable message describing the error.
:vartype message: Optional[str]
:ivar template_data: Optional variables passed to the template when rendering.
:vartype template_data: Optional[dict]


----------------------------------------------------------------------
This is the User Guide documentation for the package.
----------------------------------------------------------------------


## Get started

### Getting Started

FastAPI answers every request with JSON unless you tell it otherwise. If you are building a site that people look at in a browser, you want server-rendered HTML, and that means a template engine wired into your view functions. fastapi-chameleon does that wiring for the [Chameleon](https://chameleon.readthedocs.io/) template language with one decorator: the view returns a `dict`, the decorator renders it through a template, and FastAPI sends the HTML.

If you prefer Jinja, use the sister project [fastapi-jinja](https://github.com/AGeekInside/fastapi-jinja) instead. The two share the same design.

## Install

```bash
uv add fastapi-chameleon
# or
pip install fastapi-chameleon
```

The package requires Python 3.10 or newer and depends only on `fastapi` and `chameleon`. You also need an ASGI server such as `uvicorn` to run the app.

## A first page

Two files are enough. The template folder is passed to `global_init()` once, and every template path you use later is relative to it.

**`main.py`**

```python
from pathlib import Path

import fastapi
import uvicorn

import fastapi_chameleon

app = fastapi.FastAPI()

# Point the engine at your template folder before any view is decorated.
BASE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
fastapi_chameleon.global_init(BASE_DIR / 'templates', auto_reload=True)


@app.get('/')
@fastapi_chameleon.template('index.pt')
def hello_world():
    return {'message': "Let's go Chameleon and FastAPI!"}


if __name__ == '__main__':
    uvicorn.run(app, host='127.0.0.1', port=8000)
```

**`templates/index.pt`**

```html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>Hello</title>
</head>
<body>
<h1>Hello world</h1>
<p>Your message is <strong>${message}</strong></p>
</body>
</html>
```

Run it with `python main.py` or `uvicorn main:app`, then open `http://127.0.0.1:8000`. Both ways work here because `global_init()` runs at import time, before the decorated view is defined.

## What you get back

The decorated function now returns a `fastapi.Response`. For the request above it carries a `200` status, a `text/html` content type, and this body:

```html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>Hello</title>
</head>
<body>
<h1>Hello world</h1>
<p>Your message is <strong>Let's go Chameleon and FastAPI!</strong></p>
</body>
</html>
```

Each key in the returned `dict` became a variable in the template, so `${message}` was replaced by the string the view returned. That is the whole contract: views return data, templates turn it into HTML.

Two things in the example are easy to miss and matter later:

- The route decorator `@app.get(...)` sits on the outside. `@fastapi_chameleon.template(...)` is applied directly to the function.
- `auto_reload=True` makes Chameleon re-read templates you edit, which is what you want while developing. Turn it off in production. See [Configuration](configuration.qmd).

## Where to go next

- [Decorating Views](views.qmd): the three decorator forms, what a view may return, redirects, and `response()`.
- [Writing Templates](templates.qmd): Chameleon syntax, shared layouts, and the project layout the name inference expects.
- [Friendly Error Pages](error-pages.qmd): replace FastAPI's JSON 404 with your own HTML page.
- [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.qmd): every error the package raises and how to fix it.
- [Testing and CI](testing.qmd): call views directly in pytest, no HTTP client needed.
- [Configuration](configuration.qmd): every `global_init()` option, verified.
- [How It Works](how-it-works.qmd): module-global engine state, decoration-time decisions, exception-based error pages.
- [FAQ](faq.qmd).


### Decorating Views

A view is any FastAPI path operation, sync or async. Decorate it with `@fastapi_chameleon.template(...)` and return a `dict`. The decorator renders the template with that dict as its variables and hands FastAPI a `fastapi.Response`.

## Decorator order

The route decorator goes on the outside and the template decorator sits directly on the function:

```python
@router.post('/')
@fastapi_chameleon.template('home/index.pt')
async def home_post(request: fastapi.Request):
    form = await request.form()
    vm = PersonViewModel(**form)
    return vm.model_dump()
```

Dependency injection keeps working. Path parameters, query parameters, `Request`, and `Depends(...)` are all resolved as usual, because the decorator preserves the view's signature with `functools.wraps` and ParamSpec-based overloads. The parameters still show up in the OpenAPI schema.

## Three ways to name the template

```python
@fastapi_chameleon.template('home/index.pt')   # explicit template file
@fastapi_chameleon.template()                  # inferred template name
@fastapi_chameleon.template                    # bare form, also inferred
```

An explicit path is resolved relative to the folder passed to `global_init()`.

When no name is given, the decorator derives one from where the view lives:

- The file is `{module}/{function_name}` under the template folder, where `module` is the last segment of the view's dotted module name.
- An `.html` file is preferred. If it does not exist, `.pt` is used.
- `def index()` in `views/home.py` resolves to `templates/home/index.html`, falling back to `templates/home/index.pt`.

The inference runs once, when the module is imported, so there is no per-request filesystem work. It also means `global_init()` must have run before the view module is imported. If it has not, the folder silently defaults to `templates` relative to the current working directory, and a later `global_init()` does not re-resolve names that were already derived. Explicit template names do not have this problem.

## What a view may return

| Return value | Result |
|---|---|
| `dict` | Rendered through the template as its variables. |
| any `fastapi.Response` | Passed through untouched. The template is skipped. |
| anything else (`None`, a Pydantic model, a list) | `FastAPIChameleonException` is raised at request time. |

Returning a `Response` is how you redirect or send JSON from a page view:

```python
@router.post('/account/login')
@fastapi_chameleon.template('account/login.pt')
async def login(request: fastapi.Request):
    user = await try_login(request)
    if user:
        return fastapi.responses.RedirectResponse('/account', status_code=302)

    return {'error': 'Invalid login'}  # re-render the form with an error
```

If you have a Pydantic model, return `model.model_dump()`. If you have a dataclass, return `dataclasses.asdict(obj)`. Forgetting the `return` statement returns `None`, which raises the exception above with the message `Invalid return type <class 'NoneType'>`.

## Non-HTML output

The decorator takes a `mimetype` for templates that are not HTML:

```python
@router.get('/sitemap.xml')
@fastapi_chameleon.template('seo/sitemap.pt', mimetype='application/xml')
def sitemap():
    return {'urls': load_urls()}
```

The decorator always answers with status `200` for a rendered dict. Error pages raised with `not_found()` or `generic_error()` ignore this `mimetype` and are always `text/html`. See [Friendly Error Pages](error-pages.qmd).

## Manual rendering with `response()`

When the decorator does not fit, for example because you need a status code other than `200` or you want to render inside a view that returns several different pages, call `response()` directly:

```python
@router.get('/report')
def report():
    return fastapi_chameleon.response('reports/summary.pt', status_code=202, title='Monthly summary')
```

It renders the template with the keyword arguments as the model and returns a `fastapi.Response` with the given `mimetype` (default `text/html`) and `status_code` (default `200`). It needs `global_init()` to have run, like everything else.

To get the rendered HTML as a plain string, for an email body or a test, use `fastapi_chameleon.engine.render(template_file, **model)`.

## Reference

- [template()](../reference/template.qmd)
- [response()](../reference/response.qmd)


### Writing Templates

Chameleon templates are HTML files with a small attribute language on top. If you have used Zope Page Templates or Pyramid, it is the same TAL and METAL. If you are coming from Jinja or Django, the first thing to unlearn is `{% %}` and `{{ }}`: Chameleon has neither. Interpolation is `${expr}` and control flow lives in `tal:` attributes on ordinary elements.

## Interpolation and expressions

Anything inside `${ }` is a Python expression evaluated against the dict your view returned:

```html
<h1>Hello, ${user.name.title()}!</h1>
<p>You have ${len(items)} item(s).</p>
```

Output is HTML-escaped by default. To insert markup you already trust, use the `structure:` prefix:

```html
<div tal:content="structure: raw_html"></div>
```

## TAL attributes

```html
<!-- Loop. The repeat variable exposes index, number, even, odd, first, last. -->
<li tal:repeat="item items" tal:attributes="class 'odd' if repeat.item.odd else 'even'">
  ${repeat.item.number}. ${item.name}
</li>

<!-- Condition. The element is omitted entirely when the expression is falsy. -->
<div tal:condition="user">Welcome back, ${user.name}.</div>
<div tal:condition="not user">Please sign in.</div>

<!-- Replace element content, or the whole element. -->
<span tal:content="message">placeholder shown in a browser preview</span>
<span tal:replace="formatted_date">2024-01-01</span>

<!-- Set attributes, semicolon-separated. Escaping is automatic. -->
<a tal:attributes="href item.url; class item.css_class">${item.name}</a>

<!-- Define a local variable. -->
<span tal:define="total sum(i.price for i in items)">Total: ${total}</span>
```

The full language is documented in the [Chameleon reference](https://chameleon.readthedocs.io/en/latest/reference.html).

## Shared layouts with METAL

METAL macros are how Chameleon does what Jinja calls template inheritance. The layout defines a macro with slots, and each page fills the slots.

**`templates/shared/layout.pt`**

```html
<html metal:define-macro="layout">
  <head><title>${title}</title></head>
  <body>
    <main metal:define-slot="content">default content</main>
  </body>
</html>
```

**`templates/home/index.pt`**

```html
<div metal:use-macro="load: ../shared/layout.pt">
  <div metal:fill-slot="content">
    <h1>${title}</h1>
  </div>
</div>
```

The `load:` expression resolves the layout relative to the current template file. The variables the view returned, `title` here, are visible inside the layout too.

## Project layout

A layout that works well, and that the template name inference expects:

```text
my_app/
├── main.py                # global_init() here, before views are imported
├── views/
│   └── home.py            # def index(...) with bare @template looks for home/index.html, then home/index.pt
├── templates/
│   ├── home/
│   │   └── index.pt
│   ├── errors/
│   │   └── 404.pt         # default target of not_found()
│   └── shared/
│       └── layout.pt      # METAL macros
└── static/
```

Both `.pt` and `.html` extensions work. Chameleon treats them the same. The inference prefers `.html` and falls back to `.pt`, so pick one convention per project and stick to it. Explicit template names can use either.

## Editing templates while the server runs

Chameleon compiles each template once and caches it. Pass `auto_reload=True` to `global_init()` during development so edits are picked up on the next request without restarting. Leave it off in production. See [Configuration](configuration.qmd).

## A note on undefined variables

Referencing a variable the view did not return raises `NameError` from Chameleon at render time, naming the missing variable. FastAPI turns that into a `500`. See [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.qmd) for the full list of errors you may hit.


### Friendly Error Pages

FastAPI answers a missing resource with a JSON body, `{"detail": "Not Found"}`. For an HTML site you want a real page instead. fastapi-chameleon gives you two functions for that: `not_found()` for the common 404, and `generic_error()` for any other status code.

## A friendly 404

```python
@router.get('/catalog/item/{item_id}')
@fastapi_chameleon.template('catalog/item.pt')
async def item(item_id: int):
    item = service.get_item_by_id(item_id)
    if not item:
        fastapi_chameleon.not_found()

    return item.model_dump()
```

This renders `templates/errors/404.pt` with status `404`. To use a different template:

```python
fastapi_chameleon.not_found(four04template_file='errors/custom_404.pt')
```

The 404 template is rendered with an empty model, so it cannot show request-specific data. Keep it static, or use `generic_error()` when you need to pass variables.

## Any status code with `generic_error()`

```python
@router.get('/catalog/item/{item_id}')
@fastapi_chameleon.template('catalog/item.pt')
async def item(item_id: int):
    item = service.get_item_by_id(item_id)
    if not item.visible_to(current_user):
        fastapi_chameleon.generic_error('errors/forbidden.pt', fastapi.status.HTTP_403_FORBIDDEN)

    return item.model_dump()
```

Pass data to the error template with `template_data`:

```python
fastapi_chameleon.generic_error('errors/500.pt', 500, template_data={'detail': 'Something went sideways.'})
```

## How they work, and where they work

Both functions always raise. `not_found()` raises `FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException` and `generic_error()` raises `FastAPIChameleonGenericException`. The `@template` decorator catches those two exceptions and renders the error template with the right status. Because the decorator does the catching, you can call either function anywhere below a decorated view: in a service, a repository, or a helper. Execution stops at the call, so code after it never runs.

The flip side is that the call must happen below a decorated view. If you call `not_found()` from an undecorated route, from middleware, or from a FastAPI dependency, nothing catches the exception and FastAPI returns a plain `500 Internal Server Error`. Either decorate that route, or raise `fastapi.HTTPException` there instead.

## What the error response looks like

| | `not_found()` | `generic_error()` |
|---|---|---|
| Status | always `404` | the `status_code` you pass |
| Template | `errors/404.pt` by default, or the one you name | the one you name |
| Model | empty | `template_data`, or empty if omitted |
| Content type | `text/html` | `text/html` |

The decorator's `mimetype` argument does not apply to error pages. A view decorated with `mimetype='application/xml'` still returns its 404 as `text/html`.

If the error template itself is missing, Chameleon raises `ValueError` while rendering it, and the client sees a `500`. Create `templates/errors/404.pt` before you first call `not_found()`.

## Reference

- [not_found()](../reference/not_found.qmd)
- [generic_error()](../reference/generic_error.qmd)
- [FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException](../reference/exceptions.FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException.qmd) and [FastAPIChameleonGenericException](../reference/exceptions.FastAPIChameleonGenericException.qmd)



## Operate

### Troubleshooting

This page lists every error you can hit when using fastapi-chameleon, what it means, and the fix. Errors raised by the package itself are `FastAPIChameleonException` or a subclass. Errors raised by Chameleon while compiling or rendering a template come through as `ValueError`, `NameError`, `AttributeError`, or one of Chameleon's own exception types. All of them surface as a `500` to the browser and a traceback in the server log, so start from the log.

## Errors from the package

### `FastAPIChameleonException: You must call global_init() before rendering templates.`

A decorated view, `response()`, or `engine.render()` ran before `global_init()`. Call `global_init(template_folder)` once at startup, in the module that creates the app, before requests are served. In tests, use a fixture that calls it and clears the engine afterwards. See [Testing and CI](testing.qmd).

### `FastAPIChameleonException: The template_folder must be specified.`

`global_init()` was called with an empty string or `None`. Pass the path to your templates folder.

### `FastAPIChameleonException: The specified template folder must be a folder, it's not: ...`

The path does not exist or is a file. The message shows the path as the package saw it. Relative paths resolve against the current working directory, which differs between `python main.py`, `uvicorn main:app`, and your test runner. Build the path from `__file__` instead:

```python
BASE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
fastapi_chameleon.global_init(BASE_DIR / 'templates')
```

### `FastAPIChameleonException: Invalid return type <class 'NoneType'>, we expected a dict or fastapi.Response as the return value.`

The view returned something other than a `dict` or a `fastapi.Response`. `NoneType` almost always means a missing `return`. Other types mean you returned a model object, a list, or a string. Convert it: `model.model_dump()` for Pydantic, `dataclasses.asdict(obj)` for dataclasses, `{'items': items}` for a list.

### `500 Internal Server Error`, log shows `FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException: The URL resulted in a 404 response.`

`not_found()` was called from code that is not below a `@template`-decorated view. The same applies to `FastAPIChameleonGenericException: The URL resulted in an error.` from `generic_error()`. Nothing caught the exception, so FastAPI returned a `500`. Decorate the route, or raise `fastapi.HTTPException(status_code=404)` from undecorated code. See [Friendly Error Pages](error-pages.qmd).

### `TypeError: 'PosixPath' object is not iterable` inside `chameleon/loader.py`

Versions up to 0.1.18 accepted a `pathlib.Path` in `global_init()` but Chameleon's loader could not use it. Upgrade, or wrap the path in `str()`. Current versions accept any `os.PathLike`.

## Errors from Chameleon

### `ValueError: Template not found: home/missing.pt.`

The template path does not exist under the folder given to `global_init()`. The path in the message is relative to that folder. Check for a typo, a wrong subfolder, or `.html` versus `.pt`. If the view uses the bare `@template` form, the expected path is `{module}/{function}.html` or `.pt`, where `module` is the last segment of the view's module name. A view named `index` in `views/home.py` wants `home/index.pt`. If the path looks right but the file is still not found, the engine may be pointing at the wrong folder because `global_init()` ran after the view module was imported. See [Decorating Views](views.qmd).

### `NameError: items`

The template referenced a variable the view did not return. Chameleon names the missing variable. Add it to the dict the view returns, or guard it in the template with `tal:condition`. The same error appears when a layout macro uses a variable that one of its pages does not provide.

### `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'upper'`

An expression inside `${ }` or a `tal:` attribute failed. Chameleon appends the expression that failed, for example `- Expression: "title.upper()"`. Fix the data the view returns or make the expression tolerate the value.

### `chameleon.exc.LanguageError` or `chameleon.exc.ExpressionError`

The template itself has a bug: an invalid `tal:` attribute such as `tal:repeat="x"` without a sequence, or a Python expression with a syntax error. These are raised the first time the template is compiled, which is the first request that uses it. The message includes the offending string and the file name.

## Behaviour that looks like a bug

### Template edits are not showing up

Templates are compiled once and cached. Pass `auto_reload=True` to `global_init()` during development. If you already did, check whether `global_init()` is being called twice: the second call is ignored unless `cache_init=False`, so the first call's settings win. See [Configuration](configuration.qmd).

### The wrong template renders, or the bare `@template` form cannot find a file that exists

Template name inference runs when the view module is imported and uses the folder configured at that moment. If `global_init()` had not run yet, the folder defaulted to `templates` relative to the current working directory and a later `global_init()` did not re-resolve the name. Move `global_init()` above the view imports, or name the template explicitly.

### My 404 page returns JSON

The request never reached a decorated view. FastAPI's router answered because no route matched. Add a catch-all route decorated with `@template` that calls `not_found()`, or register a FastAPI exception handler for `404` that returns `fastapi_chameleon.response('errors/404.pt', status_code=404)`.

### The error page itself fails with a `500`

The error template is missing or broken. `not_found()` renders `errors/404.pt` by default, so create that file. A `ValueError: Template not found: errors/404.pt.` in the log confirms this cause.

## Fix order

Work from the outside in: make sure `global_init()` runs once, first, with an absolute path. Then check the view returns a dict. Then check the template path. Then read Chameleon's message for the variable or expression it names.


### Testing and CI

Decorated views stay plain Python callables. You can call them directly in a test, without `TestClient` or a running server, and inspect the `fastapi.Response` they return. This is how the package tests itself.

## A fixture for the engine

Engine state is module-global, so give each test a fresh engine and clear it afterwards:

```python
# conftest.py
from pathlib import Path

import pytest

import fastapi_chameleon as fc


@pytest.fixture
def setup_global_template(pytestconfig):
    fc.global_init(Path(pytestconfig.rootdir, 'tests', 'templates'))
    yield
    fc.engine.clear()  # do not leak engine state between tests
```

Two details keep this reliable:

- `global_init()` ignores repeat calls by default. If a test calls it directly with a different folder, pass `cache_init=False`.
- Always clear in teardown. A test that asserts "rendering before `global_init()` raises" will pass or fail depending on what ran before it otherwise.

## Calling views directly

```python
# test_views.py
import asyncio

import fastapi

import fastapi_chameleon as fc


def test_index_renders(setup_global_template):
    @fc.template('home/index.pt')
    def index(name: str):
        return {'name': name}

    resp = index('Sam')
    assert isinstance(resp, fastapi.Response)
    assert resp.status_code == 200
    assert resp.media_type == 'text/html'
    assert 'Sam' in resp.body.decode('utf-8')


def test_async_index_renders(setup_global_template):
    @fc.template('home/index.pt')
    async def index(name: str):
        return {'name': name}

    resp = asyncio.run(index('Sam'))
    assert resp.status_code == 200


def test_missing_item_gives_404(setup_global_template):
    @fc.template('home/index.pt')
    def item(item_id: int):
        fc.not_found()

    resp = item(42)
    assert resp.status_code == 404
```

Pass view arguments positionally or by keyword, exactly as FastAPI would. If a view takes a `Request`, build one with `fastapi.Request(scope)` or use `TestClient` for that test.

## Through FastAPI

When you want to test routing, dependencies, and middleware together, use FastAPI's `TestClient` against the real app. Decorated views need nothing special:

```python
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

from my_app.main import app


def test_home_page():
    client = TestClient(app)
    resp = client.get('/')
    assert resp.status_code == 200
    assert resp.headers['content-type'].startswith('text/html')
```

Make sure `global_init()` runs when `my_app.main` is imported, or call it in a session fixture before the app is created.

## CI

The package has no compiled parts, so CI is a pytest run per interpreter. A GitHub Actions matrix:

```yaml
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        python-version: ['3.10', '3.11', '3.12', '3.13', '3.14']
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v5
      - run: uv run --python ${{ matrix.python-version }} --with pytest --with-editable . pytest
```

Locally, `tox` with the `tox.ini` in the repository does the same thing across whichever interpreters you have installed.


### Configuration

All configuration happens through `global_init()`. There are no environment variables, no settings file, and no command-line interface.

## `global_init()` parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| `template_folder` | `str` or `os.PathLike` | required | Root folder for every template path. Must exist and be a directory, otherwise `FastAPIChameleonException` is raised. |
| `auto_reload` | `bool` | `False` | When `True`, Chameleon checks template files for changes on each use and recompiles them. When `False`, each template is compiled once per process. |
| `cache_init` | `bool` | `True` | When `True`, a call made after the engine is already initialized is ignored. When `False`, the call replaces the loader and folder. |

Each row was checked against the code and by running it. The `auto_reload` flag is passed straight to Chameleon's `PageTemplateLoader`.

## Calling `global_init()` more than once

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| Second call, `cache_init=True` (default) | Silently ignored. The first folder and `auto_reload` setting stay in effect. |
| Second call, `cache_init=False` | New loader and folder take effect for every template rendered from now on. |
| `engine.clear()` then `global_init()` | Same as a first call. |

A consequence worth knowing: you cannot change `auto_reload` by calling `global_init()` again with the default `cache_init`. Pass `cache_init=False` or call `fastapi_chameleon.engine.clear()` first.

## Development versus production

```python
import os
from pathlib import Path

import fastapi_chameleon

dev_mode = os.environ.get('APP_ENV', 'dev') == 'dev'  # your own switch, the package reads no env vars

BASE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
fastapi_chameleon.global_init(BASE_DIR / 'templates', auto_reload=dev_mode)
```

With `auto_reload=False`, Chameleon compiles each template to Python the first time it is used and reuses the compiled version for the life of the process. That is the setting you want under load. With `auto_reload=True`, every use checks the file's modification time, which is cheap but not free.

## The decorator

`@template(template_file=None, mimetype='text/html')` has two options:

| Parameter | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `template_file` | `None` | Template path relative to the folder. `None` means infer `{module}/{function}.html`, then `.pt`. |
| `mimetype` | `'text/html'` | Content type of the response for a rendered `dict`. Ignored for error pages. |

There is no `status_code` parameter on the decorator. A rendered dict is always a `200`. Use `response()` for another status, or `generic_error()` for error pages.

## Where `global_init()` goes

Call it at import time in the module that creates the app, before the view modules are imported. If views are registered in a separate module, the order looks like this:

```python
# main.py
import fastapi
import fastapi_chameleon

app = fastapi.FastAPI()
fastapi_chameleon.global_init('templates')

from views import home  # noqa: E402  imported after init on purpose

app.include_router(home.router)
```

The order matters only for views that let the decorator infer the template name. Views with explicit template names resolve them at request time against whatever folder is configured then.



## Understand

### How It Works

The whole library is three small modules. Knowing what happens at import time versus request time explains every gotcha in the other pages.

## Module-global engine state

`global_init()` stores two module-level values in `fastapi_chameleon.engine`: a Chameleon `PageTemplateLoader` and the template folder path. Every render goes through that one loader. There is one engine per process, which is why `global_init()` is called once and why tests clear it between runs with `engine.clear()`.

## Decoration time

`@template(...)` runs when the view module is imported. At that moment it decides three things:

1. **Which template.** An explicit name is kept as-is. A missing name is derived from the view's module and function name, and the `.html` or `.pt` choice is made by checking the filesystem once.
2. **Sync or async.** `inspect.iscoroutinefunction` picks a synchronous or asynchronous wrapper. The wrapper calls or awaits the view, then renders.
3. **The signature.** The wrapper is wrapped with `functools.wraps`, and `template()` is typed with ParamSpec-based overloads, so FastAPI's dependency injection and type checkers see the original parameters.

Because the template folder is read at decoration time for name inference, `global_init()` has to run before the view module is imported. If it has not, the folder defaults to `templates` relative to the current working directory.

## Request time

The wrapper calls the view and looks at the return value:

- A `fastapi.Response` is returned as-is.
- A `dict` is passed to the loader as the template model and the HTML comes back in a `fastapi.Response` with the decorator's `mimetype` and status `200`.
- Anything else raises `FastAPIChameleonException`.

Rendering before `global_init()` has run raises `FastAPIChameleonException` too. A template file that does not exist raises `ValueError` from Chameleon's loader.

## Error pages are exceptions

`not_found()` and `generic_error()` do not return. They raise `FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException` or `FastAPIChameleonGenericException`, both subclasses of `FastAPIChameleonException`. The wrapper catches exactly those two types and renders the error template with the status carried by the exception, always as `text/html`. Any other exception propagates to FastAPI as usual.

This is why the functions work from anywhere below a decorated view, and why they do nothing useful outside one.

## Template caching

Chameleon compiles each template to a Python module on first use and keeps it in memory. With `auto_reload=False` that compiled version is used for the rest of the process. With `auto_reload=True` the loader checks the file's modification time before each use and recompiles when it changed.

## Source

The code is short and readable: [engine.py](https://github.com/mikeckennedy/fastapi-chameleon/blob/main/fastapi_chameleon/engine.py) and [exceptions.py](https://github.com/mikeckennedy/fastapi-chameleon/blob/main/fastapi_chameleon/exceptions.py).


## Can I use Jinja instead of Chameleon?

Not with this package. Use [fastapi-jinja](https://github.com/AGeekInside/fastapi-jinja), which has the same shape: one `global_init()`, one `@template` decorator, views return dicts.

## Does it work with `APIRouter`?

Yes. Put `@router.get(...)` on the outside and `@fastapi_chameleon.template(...)` directly on the function, exactly as with `@app.get(...)`.

## Do async views work?

Yes. The decorator detects a coroutine function at decoration time and awaits it. Nothing else changes.

## Can I return a Pydantic model from a view?

No. Return `model.model_dump()`. Only a `dict` or a `fastapi.Response` is accepted, and anything else raises `FastAPIChameleonException`.

## How do I pass the request to the template?

Put it in the dict: `return {'request': request, 'title': 'Home'}`. The template can then read `${request.url.path}` or anything else on it.

## Can I have more than one template folder?

Not at the same time. There is one loader per process. Use subfolders of a single root and refer to them in template paths, such as `admin/users.pt`.

## Why does my 404 page come back as JSON, or as a 500?

Because `not_found()` was called from code that is not below a `@template`-decorated view. The decorator is what turns the exception into a page. Decorate the route, or raise `fastapi.HTTPException(404)` from undecorated code. See [Friendly Error Pages](error-pages.qmd).

## Why are my template edits not showing up?

`auto_reload` is `False` by default and templates are compiled once. Pass `auto_reload=True` to `global_init()` while developing. Note that a second `global_init()` call does not change the setting unless you pass `cache_init=False`. See [Configuration](configuration.qmd).

## Can I use the template name inference?

Yes, but call `global_init()` before importing your view modules, and keep your template folder organised as `{module}/{function}.pt`. See [Decorating Views](views.qmd). If you want fewer surprises, name templates explicitly.

## What Python versions are supported?

Python 3.10 and newer. The test suite runs on 3.10 through 3.15.

## Where is the full list of errors?

[Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.qmd) lists every exception the package raises, what it means, and how to fix it.
